1 Moriz Henneberger (1878-1959)

I recently stumbled over a minimalist but charming study by the Swiss composer Moriz Henneberger (see below). I then looked at Henneberger’s studies in more detail. Among others, Mario Garcia has cooked and corrected some of Henneberger’s studies.

A major part of Henneberger’s studies shows the rook-desperado theme. Checking these studies is somewhat tricky because often there are various ways to win. In most cases, however, the winning idea remains the same; that is, the alternative winning moves are minor duals.

Below is a summary of findings.

1.1 Two knights vs. rook and knight (GBR 0305.00)

HHdbVI has 34 studies with the GBR material 0305.00 in the starting position. The first two studies were composed by Henri Rinck in National-Zeitung (Basel, Switerland) in 1923. Both turned out to be incorrect. Moriz Henneberger was certainly inspired by Rinck’s studies. His study has a surprising first move. As often the case with Hennebergers studies, it is rather sketchy in that it has no introduction.

My study has a three-move introduction. However, endgame tablebases are needed to understand why White’s way to draw is unique. The study shows the richness of chess endgames…

Here are the two technical terms used in the Syzygy endgame tablebase; the link is syzygy

  • DTZ (distance to zeroing): the number of half-moves (ply) until a pawn move or a capture.
  • DTM (distance to mate): the number of half-moves (ply) to mate

The number of moves required to refute the White tries is mind-boggling!

1.2.1 Henneberger +0301.32a1a7 (1908). Correction

Dropping the black pawn on a5 makes the study correct and makes the study more interesting due to the try 1. Nf7.

3.1 Awards

3.1.1 Gatti 10-AT (2026)

GBR: +0322.351e1d FEN: 3k4/3Bp3/1P1r2P1/2p5/6Np/p1Pp4/5B2/4K1N1 w - - 0 1

1. g7 (1. b7? Kc7 2. Bxc5 a2 3. Bxd6+ exd6 4. g7 a1=Q+ 5. Kd2 Qb2+ 6. Kxd3 Qb1+ 7. Kd2 Qb2+ =) 1… Rg6 2. Be6! (2. g8=Q+? Rxg8 3. Be6 Rxg4 4. Bxc5 (4. Ba2? Rg2 -/+) 4… Re4+ =) 2… Rxe6+ 3. Ne5! Rxe5+ 4. Be3! Rxe3+ 5. Ne2! Rxe2+ 6. Kf1 a2 (6… Kd7 7. g8=Q Kc6 8. Qd8 +-) 7. g8=Q+ Kd7 8. Qd5+ Ke8 9. Qa8+ Kf7 10. b7 1-0.

Daniele Gatti:

Watching this study unfold feels a bit like listening to a chess lesson between a father and his little daughter. “Come on,” she says, eyes sparkling, “let’s sacrifice another piece!” The father hesitates. He looks at the board, at the King, at the growing danger. “Careful,” he replies. “We’re giving up a lot of material already. Let’s not exaggerate.” But the girl insists. And the board seems to agree with her. White begins innocently enough with 1.g7, pushing the pawn forward with confidence. Black resists, but after 2.Be6!, the sacrifices start to pile up. Each time the father frowns: “Are you sure? That’s another piece gone…” Rook after Rook is taken, Bishops step into fire, Knights jump in to be doomed. With 3.Ne5!, 4.Be3!, 5.Ne2!, White calmly offers everything. The white King, meanwhile, is becoming more and more uncomfortable. Space shrinks, flight squares disappear, and suddenly there is a serious threat of checkmate. Now the father finally loses his patience. “All right,” he says, “this is enough. You’ve sacrificed too much. Look at our position!” The girl smiles. “Don’t worry. Now watch.” With perfect timing, the pawn queens: 7.g8=Q+. The tension dissolves instantly. What looked like recklessness is revealed as careful planning. The newly born Queen takes over the board with just a few precise checks, and after 10. b7, the win is beyond doubt. A charming and instructive study: a cascade of sacrifices that never lose control, guided by a clear final idea. What at first seems like childish enthusiasm, a memory of times when all was simpler, turns out to be deep calculation — and the father, in the end, can only nod in quiet admiration. Exactly as the judge does, every time he replays this study.

Daniele Gatti:

A study with natural play and a surprising rook domination in spite of his large mobility. The Author was inspired by a real game, citing his words: “The study was inspired by the game Megan Paragua (12 years old!!) vs. Rose Atwell (16 years old!) of round 7 of the US Women’s Championship 2025, in which Megan was trying to trick Rose in a lost endgame. For more details, see the commentary by Katerina Nemcova, Yasser Seirawan, and Maurice Ashley on the YouTube video (starting at 3:15:10) of the Saint Louis Chess Club.” The game-like configuration is well recognizable and very well adapted in study form.

Eduard Eilazyan:

There are several interesting moments in this study. After the black queen appears on the board, White creates a pin and a battery with a single move: 5.Qe8! Very impressive! The next move, 6.Ke6+!, creates the effect of foresight in the form of a preliminary action. The goal of this logical maneuver is to transfer the black king to the critical a5-square, which decides the outcome of the battle in White’s favor.

Daniele Gatti:

A schematic construction, yet one that presents a clear and interesting thematic idea. The reciprocal zugzwang motif is handled with precision, and the alternation of roles between the sides is effectively demonstrated. While the execution follows a relatively familiar pattern, the study retains its appeal through clarity and logical consistency. The economy of means and the clean presentation of the central concept contribute positively to its overall impression.

Arpad Rusz:

Perpetual pursuit of the bishop by a rook. What is new compared to the previous works? In this study, in addition to a new geometry, the chase can switch its sense of rotation from counter-clockwise to clockwise!
